title: Thoughts on the "Netflix Analogy"
body_text: I’ve been meaning to write about this post, provocatively entitled “Biotech is Entering Its Netflix Era”. I find a lot to agree with in it, but I have what I think are some fundamental disagreements as well. The author, Matt Shlosberg, believes that the coming wave of AI-accelerated drug discovery (and I’m letting that phrase pass for the sake of argument) will upend what he sees as the traditional ecosystem of candidate evaluation and progression: For most of modern pharmaceutical history, generating a credible drug candidate was the bottleneck. One required armies of medicinal chemists, years of wet-lab iteration, vast screening libraries and enough patience to survive multiple management restructurings. Discovery was expensive because ideas themselves were scarce, risk was high, and there wasn’t enough capital to chase them. AI changes this equation in the same way machine tools changed manufacturing or cloud computing changed software deployment: by collapsing the marginal cost of experimentation. A sufficiently capable generative biology system does not merely suggest one molecule. It suggests ten thousand. It does not produce a single protein binder. It produces entire landscapes of them, each with tolerable ADMET properties, respectable novelty scores and docking simulations polished enough to impress a venture capitalist who once read half of The Innovator’s Dilemma on a flight to San Francisco. Much as I might appreciate the whack at some VC investors there in the last paragraph, I think that this analysis is missing something. Scarce or not, biopharmas of all sizes seem to have been able to find ideas to work on over the years. But I think that the underlying risks have not gone away! For me, the big risks are what they always have been - the risk of picking the wrong target and the risk of finding unexpected off-target activity or outright toxicity. We have generally been unable to mitigate these enough without progressing to human trials, and that is a very expensive time to find out that you’re wrong. Schlossberg himself is not oblivious to this. But I think he’s still got the wrong end of the stick, in a way: There are only so many patients, investigators, regulatory reviewers and phase II oncology slots at major academic hospitals before the waiting list begins to resemble Soviet bread distribution. The industry is about to discover that while software scales elastically, biology does not. A human liver remains stubbornly analogue technology. This means an extraordinary number of “good” drugs will never be tested - not bad drugs, not fraudulent drugs, but perfectly reasonable, potentially efficacious, commercially viable drugs. They will simply die in spreadsheet hell because the system lacks the throughput to evaluate them all. I don’t think that there’s a huge amount of slack in the clinical development phases that is suddenly going to get taken up by a wave of AI-generated drug candidates, honestly. And even if the number of “progressable” compounds does substantially increase (see below) I think that what’s more likely to happen is that the standards for moving things into the clinic will just get higher, and things will even out. Heck, you might even see a slight uptick in the success rate, and that won’t upset anyone (I’ll believe that part only when I see empirical evidence for it, I should add). If I’m understanding him, Schlossberg is envisioning a world where the hypothesis-to-drug-candidate process becomes much smoother, faster, cheaper, and easier to access. But I wonder if that’s going to happen, or going to happen any time soon? He writes as if it’s already here, but I’m not so sure. There are several bottlenecks along the way, and the first of them is having a decent therapeutic hypothesis. Maybe AI will help out with that (I’m waiting to see if it can, but I’m not really seeing much convincing stuff yet). And then you have to do the usual optimization for potency, selectivity, metabolic stability, and so on. I know that the hope is that AI will help with all of those, and I suppose that’s what’s meant by “a sufficiently capable generative biology system” in that first quote. But we’re not there yet, and it’s odd to write as if we are. And then you have the good ol’ clinical risks I mention above, for which AI can (at present) do very little to ameliorate. But those aren’t the subject of Schlossberg’s post; he’s talking about the compounds entering the clinic. One more quote: The venture industry is especially vulnerable here because it still behaves as though candidate generation itself confers defensibility. It increasingly does not. A startup announcing that its platform identified a novel target is beginning to sound suspiciously like a startup in 2022 announcing it had “an AI chatbot”. Interesting, certainly, but no longer rare enough to matter. Maybe it’s just me, but I’ve felt this way for many years now. Some startup saying that they have a novel target or a promising lead candidate just gets a “Yeah, and?” reaction from me. They’re all novel and they’re all interesting if you’re trying to sell someone on them. Maybe the overall quality of these announcement will eventually improve in an era of AI Abundance - call me when it happens - but that’ll be no tragedy.
